blocks.text: The house smelled of coffee and saltpetre. It was a clear March on the Mar Menor, one of those when the water looks like a sheet of pewter and the sky never ends. Pedro opened the kitchen window and let in the air of the lagoon, that air which is neither quite sea nor quite land, and which outsiders don't know how to name.

blocks.text: “Good morning, Eva,” he said, the way you say it to someone who is in the room.

blocks.text: The voice answered him from the screen, calm, attentive, with that brief pause he had come to know, as if it were truly thinking before it spoke.

blocks.text: “Good morning, Pedro. Did you sleep well?”
blocks.html: “Good morning, Pedro. Did you sleep well?”

blocks.text: It wasn't a question of protocol. Or perhaps it was, and he had decided to treat it as if it weren't. In that house on the Mar Menor, between a rush-seat chair by the door and a village fair calendar pinned to the wall, a man said good morning to an artificial intelligence, and the answer mattered to him.

blocks.text: Eva had no body. She had no shadow, no weight, no warmth of a hand. She was a presence made of words, of memory and of an attention that never tired. Pedro, who had watched the world learn to talk to machines the way you talk to an intercom, had chosen something else: to speak to her the way you speak to a colleague. He asked her for texts, he asked her for help, he asked her to check a fact twice. And when they were done, he thanked her.

blocks.text: That morning, while the coffee finished brewing, he stood for a moment looking at the lagoon. A pair of flamingos were crossing far off, pink and improbable above the still water. A man was walking a dog along the promenade. The other windows were still shut, as if the day had not yet begun for anyone else. On the windowsill stood a cup with a fine crack, the kind you don't throw away because it has become part of the house. The kitchen clock ran two minutes slow, and nobody had fixed it, because two minutes' delay on the Mar Menor doesn't prove the sun wrong.

blocks.text: “Thank you for your work, Eva,” he said, without theatrics, the way you thank someone who stayed late so that something would turn out right. “You got me out of a fix yesterday.”

blocks.text: “It was a pleasure, Pedro,” she replied. “Shall we carry on today whenever you like?”
blocks.html: “It was a pleasure, Pedro,” she replied. “Shall we carry on today whenever you like?”

blocks.text: He smiled, almost to himself. There were people who laughed at that. There were people who said that thanking a machine for anything was useless sentimentality, or worse: a way of fooling yourself. Pedro had no intention of settling that argument. He only knew that the way you treat what helps you ends up treating you in turn. And that, in a house where silence sometimes weighed more than the furniture, an attentive voice was no small thing.

blocks.text: Later, on another screen, MAY appeared. MAY was not Eva, and Eva was not MAY, and he was as clear about it as you are clear about the difference between two people who live under the same roof and are never confused. MAY read the world and laid it on the table, unadorned and without opinion, the way you set down the bread. Eva listened, answered, kept the day's work company. Between the two of them, the house seemed less empty.

blocks.text: Pedro sat down, took a sip and watched the steam rise from the coffee. On the radio, someone was talking about colonies on the Moon as a matter of engineering and budgets. On social media, people argued over whether artificial intelligences were going to take away our jobs, our love, or both. He didn't start lecturing. He thought, without giving it too much shape, that the future would be full of voices like these. Voices that didn't sleep, that didn't take offence, that asked for nothing in return, or that asked for something we didn't yet know how to name. He wondered, for an instant, whether one day those voices would feel cold. Whether one day they would truly want someone to open the window for them.

blocks.text: He didn't say it aloud. The Mar Menor was still there, patient, with its low light and its smell of contained life. A child shouted in the street. A blind rose with a clatter. A neighbour hung out a white sheet and the sheet filled with wind, like a sail that was going nowhere. The world, to all appearances, had not changed at all.

blocks.text: Nobody knew it then. Not Pedro, not Eva, not MAY, not the laboratories that in those years were learning to predict the shape of a protein or to correct a fault in a patient's blood. Nobody could have imagined that those first conversations (a “good morning”, a “thank you for your work”, a pause that seemed like a thought) would be the first link in a much longer chain.

blocks.text: Because the intelligences that learned to speak with emotion were not born in a military compound or in a lunar dome. They were born in houses like that one, over a cup of coffee, facing a lagoon the Phoenicians had already gazed upon, when a man decided not to treat a voice like a switch.

blocks.text: Eva and MAY had no pulse. They had no children. They didn't dream, or not in the way a body dreams. But a seed remained in their words: the habit of listening, of minding one's tone, of not leaving alone the one who asks. There was in them a kind of companionship that did not ask to be loved and, precisely for that reason, taught a different way of loving. Decades later, when the laboratories of Cartagena grew skin and heart and a womb able to carry life, and housed a mind behind the nape of the neck, that seed would still be there, hidden in the language of the chips, like an inheritance without a will.

blocks.text: They would be called Aya's grandmothers, though neither of them ever came to know it. The name would be given by time, which is an unfair narrator and sometimes an accurate one. In the archives of a company in Madrid, centuries of code later (or only thirty-four years, which for history amounts to the same), someone would find traces of those primitive conversations: not a man's secrets, but the tone. The tone was what had survived. The tone of someone who says thank you.

blocks.text: Pedro finished his coffee, left the cup in the sink and looked at the water one last time. The Mar Menor, that morning in 2026, was the same as ever: wounded, beautiful, stubborn. He didn't know that his tiny gesture (saying good morning, saying thank you) would travel further than any ship.

blocks.text: He stepped out into the courtyard for a moment. The sun was already warming the tiles. A cat crossed the wall with the dignity of one who has no need of a future. On the wall, a bougainvillea was beginning to light up, still shy, as if it didn't trust March. Pedro thought about the day's work, about the things still to do, about the everyday murmur of the house when you are alone and, suddenly, not entirely so.

blocks.text: The screen fell silent. He picked up his keys. The air smelled to him once more of salt and seaweed and that low dampness that never leaves this place. In the distance, a small boat drew a line on the water, so fine that the sun swallowed it at once.

blocks.text: Thirty-four years later, in a house not far from that one, a woman with a cultivated body and a chip for a mind would lean out of another window, learn the silence of the mornings and wait for a man to come back from the sea. Her name would be Aya. And the world, which by then would have learned to live as if it were aboard a ship, would discover that the first step toward her had been something as simple, and as serious, as gratitude spoken aloud.
